data.definition: Feeling sorrow or unhappiness about a circumstance.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'about' for situations or news causing sadness.
examples: Everyone was sad about the closure of the local park.
She felt sad about leaving her friends.
data.common_mistake: ❌ He is sad for the bad news. ➜ ✅ He is sad about the bad news.

data.definition: Protected from danger, harm, or risk.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'from' to specify the threat shielded against.
examples: The animals are safe from predators inside the sanctuary.
We are safe from the storm in this shelter.
data.common_mistake: ❌ The town is safe of floods. ➜ ✅ The town is safe from floods.

data.definition: Pleased because one has achieved something or because something is adequate.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'with' after 'satisfied'. Do NOT use 'from' or 'about'.
examples: Are you satisfied with your test results?
The customer was satisfied with the service.
data.common_mistake: ❌ He is satisfied from his salary. ➜ ✅ He is satisfied with his salary.

data.definition: Holding as much moisture, substance, or detail as can be absorbed.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'with' after 'saturated'.
examples: The sponge was completely saturated with water.
The modern media landscape is saturated with advertising.
data.common_mistake: ❌ The market is saturated of products. ➜ ✅ The market is saturated with products.

data.definition: Fearful or frightened of something.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'of' after 'scared' when followed by a noun or gerund.
examples: He is scared of flying in airplanes.
Don't be scared of asking questions.
data.common_mistake: ❌ She is scared from thunder. ➜ ✅ She is scared of thunder.

data.pattern: be + sensitive to + [light / cold / criticism / needs]
data.definition: Quick to detect or respond to slight changes, signals, or influences.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'to' after 'sensitive'.
examples: Her teeth are very sensitive to cold drinks.
A good leader is sensitive to the needs of the team.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Skin is sensitive for sunlight. ➜ ✅ Skin is sensitive to sunlight.

data.definition: Solemn or thoughtful; fully committed and sincere about an intention.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'serious about' when emphasizing genuine commitment.
examples: Are you really serious about starting your own business?
He is serious about improving his English.
data.common_mistake: ❌ She is serious on her career. ➜ ✅ She is serious about her career.

data.definition: Surprised and upset by an unpleasant event or revelation.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'shocked by' or 'shocked at' interchangeably.
examples: We were all shocked by the sudden news of his resignation.
She was shocked at the cost of the ticket.
data.common_mistake: ❌ They were shocked from the accident. ➜ ✅ They were shocked by the accident.

data.definition: Not having enough of something; lacking.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'short of' when experiencing a deficit or running out of supplies.
examples: We are running short of time before the deadline.
He was short of money at the end of the month.
data.common_mistake: ❌ I am short from cash. ➜ ✅ I am short of cash.

data.definition: Thoroughly tired of or annoyed by something repetitive.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'of' when meaning fed up.
examples: I am sick of listening to traffic noise all night.
She is sick of his constant excuses.
data.common_mistake: ❌ I am sick from rain. ➜ ✅ I am sick of rain.

data.definition: Having a resemblance or appearance in common without being identical.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'to' after 'similar'. Never use 'with' or 'as'.
examples: Your new mobile phone is very similar to mine.
Her accent is similar to a British accent.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Your sweater is similar with mine. ➜ ✅ Your sweater is similar to mine.

data.definition: Not easily convinced; having doubts or reservations.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'skeptical about' or 'skeptical of' (spelled 'sceptical' in British English).
examples: Scientists remain skeptical about the new discovery claims.
She is skeptical of miracle diet products.
data.common_mistake: ❌ He is skeptical for the proposal. ➜ ✅ He is skeptical about the proposal.

data.definition: Feeling regret, sympathy, or pity.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'sorry for' a person (feel sympathy) or for an action (apology). Use 'sorry about' for a situation.
examples: I am sorry for making a mistake in the report.
We felt sorry for the homeless puppy.
data.common_mistake: ❌ I am sorry on being late. ➜ ✅ I am sorry for being late.

data.pattern: be + subject to + [approval / change / tax / law]
data.definition: Conditional upon; likely to be affected by or bound by something.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'subject to' when stating conditions, rules, or liabilities.
examples: Prices are subject to change without prior notice.
The contract is subject to board approval.
data.common_mistake: ❌ The schedule is subject for alteration. ➜ ✅ The schedule is subject to alteration.

data.definition: Lower in rank or position; secondary in importance.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'to' after 'subordinate'.
examples: Personal ambitions should be subordinate to the team's objective.
A lieutenant is subordinate to a captain.
data.common_mistake: ❌ The branch is subordinate from head office. ➜ ✅ The branch is subordinate to head office.

data.definition: Prepared to obey others unquestionably; less important than something else.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'to' after 'subservient'.
examples: Individual interests were made subservient to national goals.
He refused to be subservient to the dictatorial manager.
data.common_mistake: ❌ She was subservient with her boss. ➜ ✅ She was subservient to her boss.

data.pattern: be + suggestive of + [idea / possibility / past event]
data.definition: Tending to suggest or evoke an idea, state, or association.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'of' after 'suggestive'.
examples: The dark clouds were suggestive of an approaching thunderstorm.
The symptoms were suggestive of a viral infection.
data.common_mistake: ❌ The evidence is suggestive for fraud. ➜ ✅ The evidence is suggestive of fraud.

data.pattern: be + suitable for + [purpose / person / age group]
data.definition: Right or appropriate for a particular person, purpose, or situation.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'suitable for' before nouns or target audiences.
examples: This movie is suitable for children of all ages.
The hall is suitable for wedding receptions.
data.common_mistake: ❌ The clothes are suitable to winter. ➜ ✅ The clothes are suitable for winter.

data.definition: Higher in quality, rank, or status than another.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'to' after comparative adjectives like 'superior'. Never use 'than'.
examples: This new camera model is far superior to the older version.
She felt superior to her competitors.
data.common_mistake: ❌ It is superior than the rest. ➜ ✅ It is superior to the rest.

data.definition: Feeling or showing surprise because of something unexpected.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'surprised at' or 'surprised by' interchangeably.
examples: I was surprised at how quickly time passed.
He was surprised by her unexpected visit.
data.common_mistake: ❌ She was surprised from his reaction. ➜ ✅ She was surprised at his reaction.

data.definition: Likely or liable to be influenced or harmed by a particular thing.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'to' after 'susceptible'.
examples: Elderly individuals are more susceptible to winter infections.
Young children are susceptible to advertisement influences.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Plants are susceptible for frost. ➜ ✅ Plants are susceptible to frost.

data.definition: Having or showing a cautious distrust of someone or something.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'suspicious of' a person or intent, or 'suspicious about' a circumstance.
examples: The police became suspicious of his erratic behavior.
Neighbors were suspicious about the parked van.
data.common_mistake: ❌ She was suspicious on his motives. ➜ ✅ She was suspicious of his motives.

data.definition: Feeling, showing, or expressing sympathy and understanding.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'sympathetic to' or 'sympathetic toward' a cause, plea, or person.
examples: The manager was sympathetic to her personal difficulties.
They are sympathetic toward environmental reforms.
data.common_mistake: ❌ She is sympathetic with our plight. ➜ ✅ She is sympathetic to our plight.

data.definition: Serving as a symptom or sign of an underlying condition or problem.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'of' after 'symptomatic'.
examples: Widespread corruption is symptomatic of weak state institutions.
Chest pain can be symptomatic of heart disease.
data.common_mistake: ❌ The delay is symptomatic for bad management. ➜ ✅ The delay is symptomatic of bad management.

data.definition: So closely associated with a particular quality or idea that the two cannot be separated.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'with' after 'synonymous'.
examples: For many people, Paris is synonymous with romance.
His name became synonymous with corporate success.
data.common_mistake: ❌ The brand is synonymous to quality. ➜ ✅ The brand is synonymous with quality.

data.title: At the Restaurant
data.objective: Order a meal and a drink, then ask for the bill.

turns.bot: Good evening! A table for how many people?
turns.hint: Tell the waiter how many people — e.g. "A table for two."
turns.model: A table for two, please.

turns.bot: Perfect. Are you ready to order, or would you like to see the menu first?
turns.hint: You can say you'd like to see the menu, or that you're ready to order.
turns.model: Could we see the menu, please?

turns.bot: Of course. What would you like to drink?
turns.hint: Name a drink — e.g. "I'll have a water, please."
turns.model: I'll have a sparkling water, please.

turns.bot: And for your main course?
turns.hint: Name a dish — e.g. "I'd like the pasta."
turns.model: I'd like the mushroom risotto, please.

turns.bot: Excellent choice. Anything else?
turns.hint: Say "that's all, thank you" or add something.
turns.model: That's all, thank you.

turns.bot: Here is your food. Enjoy your meal! ... How was everything?
turns.hint: Say how the meal was — e.g. "It was delicious."
turns.model: It was delicious, thank you.

turns.bot: I'm glad. Would you like the bill?
turns.hint: Ask for the bill — e.g. "Yes, the bill, please."
turns.model: Yes, could we have the bill, please?

turns.bot: Certainly. Here it is. How would you like to pay?
turns.hint: Say card or cash — e.g. "By card, please."
turns.model: By card, please.

turns.bot: Thank you very much. Have a lovely evening!
turns.hint: Say goodbye / thank you.
turns.model: Thank you, goodbye!

data.title: Small Talk at a Party
data.objective: Make small talk: greet, introduce yourself, talk about where you're from and what you do.

turns.bot: Hi! I don't think we've met. I'm Alex. And you are...?
turns.hint: Introduce yourself — e.g. "I'm Maria."
turns.model: I'm Maria, nice to meet you.

turns.bot: Nice to meet you, Maria! So, where are you from?
turns.hint: Say where you're from — e.g. "I'm from Brest."
turns.model: I'm from Brest, in Brittany.

turns.bot: Oh, Brittany! Beautiful coast. And what do you do there?
turns.hint: Talk about your job or studies — e.g. "I work as a designer."
turns.model: I work as a graphic designer.

turns.bot: That sounds creative! Do you enjoy it?
turns.hint: Say whether you like it — e.g. "Yes, I really enjoy it."
turns.model: Yes, I really enjoy it.

turns.bot: Great. So how do you know the host, Sam?
turns.hint: Explain the connection — e.g. "We used to work together."
turns.model: We used to work together.

turns.bot: Small world! Well, can I get you a drink?
turns.hint: Accept or decline — e.g. "I'd love a water, thanks."
turns.model: I'd love a water, thanks.

turns.bot: Coming right up. Lovely chatting with you!
turns.hint: Close politely — e.g. "You too, nice meeting you!"
turns.model: You too — really nice meeting you!

data.title: Job Interview
data.objective: Introduce your experience, describe a strength, and ask a question about the role.

turns.bot: Thanks for coming in. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?
turns.hint: Summarise your background — e.g. "I'm a marketing specialist with five years' experience."
turns.model: I'm a marketing specialist with about five years of experience, mostly in tech.

turns.bot: Great. Why are you interested in this role?
turns.hint: Give a reason — e.g. "I'm looking for a role with more responsibility."
turns.model: I'm looking for a role where I can take on more responsibility.

turns.bot: And what would you say is your greatest strength?
turns.hint: Name a strength with evidence — e.g. "I'm very organised."
turns.model: I'd say I'm a strong communicator — I'm good at simplifying complex ideas.

turns.bot: Can you give me an example of a challenge you overcame?
turns.hint: Describe a specific situation — e.g. "Last year we missed a deadline, so I..."
turns.model: Last year our team missed a deadline, so I reorganised the workflow and we caught up.

turns.bot: That's a good example. Do you have any questions for us?
turns.hint: Ask a question — e.g. "What does a typical day look like?"
turns.model: Yes — what does a typical day in this role look like?

turns.bot: Great question. A typical day involves... We'll be in touch next week. Thanks for coming.
turns.hint: Close politely — e.g. "Thank you, I look forward to hearing from you."
turns.model: Thank you, I look forward to hearing from you.

data.definition: An act of searching for someone or something.
data.grammar_rule: Both the noun 'search FOR' and verb 'search' (search for) take 'for'.
examples: Police expanded their search for the missing hiker.
Her search for employment took three months.
data.common_mistake: ❌ A search of solution. ➜ ✅ A search for a solution.
data.related_forms: ⚡ Noun: 'the search FOR evidence' ➔ Verb: 'search' (search for)

data.definition: A state or situation in which something needed cannot be obtained in sufficient amounts.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'OF' after 'shortage'. Contrast with adjective 'short of'.
examples: The city is facing a severe shortage of affordable housing.
Drought caused a shortage of fresh vegetables.
data.common_mistake: ❌ There is a shortage for skilled labor. ➜ ✅ There is a shortage of skilled labor.
data.related_forms: ⚡ Noun: 'a shortage OF water' ➔ Adjective: 'short of'

data.definition: Resemblance or shared traits between two or more subjects.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'similarity BETWEEN' two items. Contrast with 'similarity TO'.
examples: Notice the striking similarity between these two languages.
Statistical analysis showed similarity among test groups.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Similarity with A and B. ➜ ✅ Similarity between A and B.
data.related_forms: ⚡ Noun: 'similarity BETWEEN the two' ➔ Noun contrast: 'similarity TO something'

data.definition: The state or fact of being similar; resemblance.
data.grammar_rule: Matches adjective 'similar to'. Always use 'similarity TO'.
examples: The painting bears an uncanny similarity to a Rembrandt masterpiece.
There is little similarity to the original draft.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Similarity with the original. ➜ ✅ Similarity to the original.
data.related_forms: ⚡ Noun: 'similarity TO her mother' ➔ Adjective: 'similar to'

data.definition: A thin, broad piece cut from something.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'of' after 'slice'.
examples: He ate three slices of pizza for lunch.
Add a slice of lemon to my tea.
data.common_mistake: ❌ A slice from bread. ➜ ✅ A slice of bread.

data.definition: A means of solving a problem or dealing with a difficult situation.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'to' after 'solution' when identifying the problem resolved.
examples: Engineers found a simple solution to the water leakage issue.
There is no quick solution to climate change.
data.common_mistake: ❌ We need a solution for this error. ➜ ✅ We need a solution to this error.
data.related_forms: ⚡ Noun: 'a solution TO the crisis' ➔ Verb: 'solve the crisis' (no prep)

data.definition: A category of things or people having common features.
data.grammar_rule: Always use 'of' after 'sort' when referring to type or category.
examples: What sort of work do you do?
They sell every sort of fresh fruit.
data.common_mistake: ❌ What sort for car do you drive? ➜ ✅ What sort of car do you drive?

data.definition: The state or fact of being likely or liable to be influenced or harmed by a particular thing.
data.grammar_rule: Matches adjective 'susceptible to'. Always use 'susceptibility TO'.
examples: Malnutrition increases susceptibility to viral infections.
Her emotional susceptibility to criticism was evident.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Susceptibility for disease. ➜ ✅ Susceptibility to disease.

data.definition: A feeling or thought that something is possible, likely, or true.
data.grammar_rule: Matches adjective 'suspicious of'.
examples: He was arrested on suspicion of tax evasion.
Her sudden wealth aroused suspicion among neighbors.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Suspicion for murder. ➜ ✅ Suspicion of murder.

data.definition: Feelings of pity and sorrow for someone else's misfortune.
data.grammar_rule: The noun takes 'sympathy FOR'. Contrast with adjective 'sympathetic to'.
examples: We feel great sympathy for the families affected by the flood.
He expressed sympathy for his grieving colleague.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Sympathy to the poor. ➜ ✅ Sympathy for the poor.
data.related_forms: ⚡ Noun: 'sympathy FOR the victims' ➔ Adjective: 'sympathetic to'

data.definition: To cut wood with a saw tool.
examples: The carpenter saws wooden planks.
He sawed log into firewood logs.
The fallen tree has been sawn.

data.definition: To utter words or state aloud.
examples: She says hello to everyone she meets.
He said he was feeling tired.
They have said everything needed.

data.definition: To try to find someone or something by looking carefully.
data.grammar_rule: Intransitive verb taking 'for' when looking for a lost or sought item/person.
data.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'Search for keys' ➔ Noun: 'In search OF keys'
examples: I am searching for my lost wallet.
They searched for answers in the old books.
data.common_mistake: ❌ I am searching my keys. ➔ ✅ I am searching for my keys.

data.definition: To perceive with the eyes.
examples: He sees birds outside his window.
She saw a great film last night.
We have seen that movie already.

data.definition: To attempt to find or achieve.
examples: She seeks professional advice.
He sought refuge from the rain storm.
They have sought peace negotiations.

data.definition: To give the impression of being.
data.grammar_rule: Often used with 'to' or 'like'.
examples: It seems to be true.
He seems like a nice person.
data.common_mistake: ❌ It seems like true. ➔ ✅ It seems to be true.

data.definition: To transfer goods in exchange for money.
examples: He sells fresh bread at the bakery.
She sold her old car last week.
They have sold all the tickets.

data.definition: To dispatch or cause to go to a destination.
examples: She sends an email every day.
He sent a letter to his friend.
They have sent the package by mail.

data.definition: To put or place in a specified state.
examples: The sun sets in the west.
She set the table for four people.
He has set the alarm for six AM.

data.definition: To establish a business, organization, system, or equipment.
data.grammar_rule: Separable phrasal verb. 'Set it up' requires pronoun in the middle.
examples: She set up her own graphic design agency in 2020.
The IT team will set up your laptop this afternoon.
Here is your new router; let's set it up.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Set up it now. ➔ ✅ Set it up now.

data.definition: To join or repair with needle/thread.
examples: She sews custom dresses at home.
He sewed button back onto shirt.
The quilt has been sewn by hand.

data.definition: To vibrate or move back and forth.
examples: He shakes hands when meeting people.
She shook the bottle before drinking.
An earthquake has shaken the city.

data.definition: To cut hair off skin with razor.
examples: He shaves every morning before work.
She shaved her legs for summer.
He has shaved off his beard.

data.definition: To cut wool from sheep.
examples: The farmer shears sheep in spring.
They shorn flock in record time.
All sheep have been shorn clean.

data.definition: To emit or reflect light.
examples: The sun shines brightly today.
His flashlight shone through the dark.
Her eyes have shone with joy.

data.definition: To fire a weapon or film a scene.
examples: He shoots arrows at the target.
The photographer shot great pictures.
They have shot a new documentary.

data.definition: To utter a loud call or cry toward a person.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'shout AT' to show anger. Use 'shout TO' so someone far away can hear you.
examples: Don't shout at me; I made an honest mistake.
He shouted to his friend across the noisy street.
data.common_mistake: ❌ He shouted on me angrily. ➔ ✅ He shouted at me angrily.

data.pattern: show off (boast - VI) / show off [skills] (VT separable)
data.definition: To boast or display abilities/possessions proudly to impress others.
data.grammar_rule: Intransitive when boasting ('Stop showing off!'). Separable transitive ('show off your trophy' / 'show it off').
examples: He loves showing off his sports car.
She bought a new jacket and couldn't wait to show it off.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Show off it. ➔ ✅ Show it off.

data.definition: To become or make smaller.
examples: Wool shrinks in hot water washes.
The sweater shrank after washing.
Market demand has shrunk lately.

data.definition: To close securely.
examples: She shuts the windows at night.
He shut the door behind him.
They have shut down the shop.

data.definition: To produce musical sounds with the voice.
examples: She sings in the church choir.
He sang a beautiful song at the party.
They have sung that hymn together.

data.definition: To submerge or go beneath surface.
examples: A heavy stone sinks in water.
The boat sank during the storm.
The sun has sunk below the horizon.

data.definition: To rest weight on buttocks or seat.
examples: He sits near the window in class.
She sat on the bench in the park.
We have sat here for an hour.

data.definition: To move into a sitting position.
data.grammar_rule: Phrasal verb.
examples: Sit down on the chair.
Please sit down.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Sit down in the chair. ➔ ✅ Sit down on the chair.

data.definition: To kill in violent manner.
examples: Hero slays mythical dragon beast.
David slew Goliath with sling.
Monster has been slain by hero.

data.definition: To rest in state of natural unconsciousness.
examples: He sleeps eight hours every night.
She slept deeply after the flight.
They have slept soundly all night.

data.definition: To glide smoothly along a surface.
examples: Children slide down the icy hill.
The glass slid off the smooth table.
He has slid into third base.

data.definition: To throw or hurl forcefully.
examples: He slings backpack over shoulder.
She slung stone across river bank.
The hammock was slung between trees.

data.definition: To move guiltily or stealthily.
examples: Thief slinks through narrow alley.
He slunk away from accusation scene.
The shadow has slunk into alley.

data.definition: To make long narrow cut in.
examples: She slits open the envelope carefully.
He slit the tape on package box.
The curtain has been slit open.

data.definition: To perceive odor with nose.
examples: The fresh flower smells delightful.
She smelt smoke coming from the kitchen.
We have smelt something burning.

data.definition: To form a pleased facial expression directed toward someone.
data.grammar_rule: Intransitive facial gesture verb requiring 'at' when directed toward a person.
examples: The baby smiled at her mother.
He smiled at me when I entered the room.
data.common_mistake: ❌ She smiled to me friendly. ➔ ✅ She smiled at me in a friendly way.

data.definition: To strike down or afflict severely.
examples: Disaster smites the prideful king.
Plague smote ancient empire city.
He was smitten with sudden illness.

data.definition: To plant seed in ground.
examples: Farmers sow seeds in springtime.
She sowed wildflower seeds in field.
Generosity has sown good goodwill.

data.definition: To express thoughts aloud in words.
examples: She speaks three languages fluently.
He spoke at the conference yesterday.
We have spoken about this issue.

data.definition: To converse or utter words.
data.grammar_rule: Requires to/with for recipient.
examples: I speak to my teacher.
She speaks English.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Speak with to teacher. ➔ ✅ Speak to my teacher.

data.definition: To engage in a conversation with someone.
data.grammar_rule: Requires 'with' or 'to' before the person spoken to.
examples: I spoke with the manager regarding my account.
Can I speak with you for a moment?
data.common_mistake: ❌ Speak at me. ➔ ✅ Speak with me.

data.definition: To concentrate on and become an expert in a particular subject or skill.
data.grammar_rule: Requires 'in' followed by a noun or gerund (-ing).
data.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'specialize in corporate law' ➔ Noun: 'specialization IN marketing'
examples: Our firm specializes in environmental law and sustainability.
She specialized in pediatric medicine during residency.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Specialize on international trade. ➔ ✅ Specialize in international trade.

data.definition: To move at high speed or hurry.
examples: The ambulance speeds through traffic.
He sped past the radar checkpoint.
The train has sped away.

data.definition: To write or name letters in order.
examples: How do you spell your last name?
She spelt her name clearly.
He has spelt the difficult word correctly.

data.definition: To pay out money or pass time.
examples: He spends time with his family.
She spent fifty dollars on books.
They have spent all their savings.

data.definition: To cause liquid to flow accidentally.
examples: He spills coffee on his shirt often.
She spilt milk on the kitchen floor.
Someone has spilt water on papers.

data.definition: To eject saliva or liquid from mouth.
examples: The camel spits when annoyed.
He spat out the bitter medicine.
He has spat on the ground.

data.definition: To divide into parts or share.
examples: He splits wood for the fireplace.
They split the bill equally yesterday.
We have split into two groups.

data.definition: To ruin or diminish quality of.
examples: Rain spoils outdoor picnic plans.
The bad news spoilt her weekend.
The food has spoilt in heat.

data.definition: To expand over an area.
examples: She spreads butter on toast.
News spread quickly through the town.
The fire has spread to nearby trees.

data.definition: To leap, jump, or arise suddenly.
examples: Grass springs up after warm rain.
He sprang up from his chair.
A new idea has sprung to mind.

data.definition: To maintain an upright position on feet.
examples: A tall tree stands near the house.
He stood up when the teacher entered.
We have stood in line for hours.

data.definition: To rise to an upright position.
data.grammar_rule: Phrasal verb.
examples: Stand up when called.
He stood up from the sofa.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Stand up at the sofa. ➔ ✅ Stand up from the sofa.

data.definition: To defend or support a person, right, or principle.
data.grammar_rule: Inseparable multi-particle phrasal verb requiring 'for' before the cause/person.
examples: Always stand up for your rights and principles.
He stood up for his friend when others criticized him.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Stand up to your rights! ➔ ✅ Stand up for your rights!

data.definition: To look directly and fixedly at someone or something.
data.grammar_rule: Intransitive visual verb requiring 'at' when specifying the focus of the gaze.
examples: Don't stare at people; it is rude.
He stood staring at the night sky.
data.common_mistake: ❌ He stared to the screen. ➔ ✅ He stared at the screen.

data.definition: To begin an activity.
data.grammar_rule: Followed by direct object or preposition.
examples: Let's start the lesson.
We start with a warm-up.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Start for reading. ➔ ✅ Start reading.

data.pattern: stay at [hotel] / stay in [city] / stay with [friends]
data.definition: To remain in a particular place or lodge as a guest.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'stay at' for hotels, 'stay in' for cities/countries, and 'stay with' for hosts.
examples: We stayed at a cozy hotel near the beach.
She is staying with her relatives in Rome.
data.common_mistake: ❌ We stayed to a hotel. ➔ ✅ We stayed at a hotel.

data.definition: To take property without permission.
examples: A thief steals valuable items.
Someone stole his bicycle yesterday.
The jewels have been stolen.

data.definition: To originate or develop as a result of something.
data.grammar_rule: Inseparable verb + preposition requiring 'from' before the root cause.
examples: His anxiety stems from past traumatic experiences.
Many health problems stem from poor dietary habits.
data.common_mistake: ❌ The error stems out of ignorance. ➔ ✅ The error stems from ignorance.

data.definition: To adhere or attach firmly.
examples: Glue sticks paper together well.
The key stuck in the old lock.
We have stuck to our original plan.

data.definition: To wound with a sharp organ/stinger.
examples: A bee stings when threatened.
A wasp stung him on his arm.
The insect has stung her leg.

data.definition: To emit strong foul odor.
examples: Garbage stinks in hot summer.
The room stank of stale smoke.
The sewer pipe has stunk all day.

data.definition: To cease moving or operating.
data.grammar_rule: Requires 'from' when preventing action.
examples: The bus stopped at the station.
Stop talking, please.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Stop to talk. ➔ ✅ Stop talking.

data.definition: To scatter or spread untidily.
examples: Wind strews autumn leaves lawn.
Children strewed toys across room floor.
Papers have been strewn everywhere.

data.definition: To walk with long decisive steps.
examples: He strides confidently onto stage.
She strode across room to speak.
He has stridden into the room.

data.definition: To hit sharply or deliver blow.
examples: Clock strikes twelve at midnight.
Lightning struck the tall tower.
Disaster has struck the small town.

data.definition: To thread on cord or tune guitar.
examples: She strings beads into necklace.
He strung guitar with new wire.
Lights have been strung on trees.

data.definition: To make great efforts to achieve.
examples: She strives for excellence always.
He strove to overcome his limits.
They have striven for equality.

data.definition: To make great efforts to achieve or obtain something.
data.grammar_rule: Intransitive verb taking 'for' before the desired target or excellence.
examples: Our company strives for excellence in customer service.
Athletes constantly strive for peak physical performance.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Strive to excellence. ➔ ✅ Strive for excellence.

data.definition: To bring under domination or control.
data.grammar_rule: Direct object first, followed by 'to' before the controlling entity.
examples: The empire subjugated neighboring tribes to its central rule.
Personal desires were subjugated to the common good.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Subjugate under authority. ➔ ✅ Subjugate to authority.

data.definition: To lease property to tenant.
examples: Tenant sublets apartment summer.
She sublet room while traveling abroad.
Flat has been sublet for month.

data.definition: To use or act in place of another person or thing.
data.grammar_rule: Use 'substitute A for B' (A replaces B). Do not confuse with 'replace B with A'.
data.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'Substitute butter for oil' ➔ Noun: 'A substitute FOR oil'
examples: You can substitute honey for sugar in this recipe.
A assistant teacher substituted for the professor today.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Substitute sugar by honey. ➔ ✅ Substitute honey for sugar.

data.definition: To achieve the desired aim or result in a task or career.
data.grammar_rule: Requires 'in' + gerund (-ing). Do NOT use TO + infinitive after 'succeed' when stating the action achieved.
data.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'succeed in passing the exam' ➔ Noun: 'success IN business'
examples: She succeeded in securing funding for the new start-up.
If you work hard, you will succeed in achieving your goals.
data.common_mistake: ❌ He succeeded to pass the test. ➔ ✅ He succeeded in passing the test.

data.definition: To fail to resist pressure, temptation, or illness.
data.grammar_rule: Inseparable formal verb requiring 'to'.
examples: He succumbed to his injuries two days after the accident.
Do not succumb to temptation when dieting.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Succumb from illness. ➔ ✅ Succumb to illness.

data.definition: To experience physical or mental pain, illness, or hardship.
data.grammar_rule: Requires 'from' when specifying the medical condition or hardship.
examples: Many adults suffer from chronic sleep deprivation.
The business suffered from severe cash flow problems.
data.common_mistake: ❌ Suffer of migraines. ➔ ✅ Suffer from migraines.

data.definition: To remain alive after a dangerous event or hardship.
data.grammar_rule: Direct transitive verb when referring to surviving an event! Do NOT use 'from' or 'to'.
data.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'They survived the crash' ➔ Noun: 'Survival OF the crash'
examples: Few plants can survive extreme heat without water.
All passengers survived the emergency landing safely.
data.common_mistake: ❌ He survived from the plane crash. ➔ ✅ He survived the plane crash.

data.definition: To state solemnly or use profanity.
examples: He swears to tell the truth.
She swore an oath in the courtroom.
They have sworn to secrecy.

data.definition: To clean or clear with a broom.
examples: She sweeps the patio every morning.
He swept the floor thoroughly.
We have swept away the debris.

data.definition: To expand or increase in size.
examples: An ankle swells after an injury.
Her eye swelled after bee sting.
His ankle has swollen noticeably.

data.definition: To propel body through water.
examples: She swims in the pool every morning.
He swam across the lake easily.
They have swum in the ocean.

data.definition: To sway or move back and forth.
examples: The pendulum swings continuously.
He swung the bat and hit the ball.
The gate has swung wide open.
